title: Mini Magazine Creator
tagline: Writing in many styles · Design · Publishing
goal: Your kid makes their own mini magazine about something they love: dinosaurs, football, baking, their pet. They plan the issue, write different kinds of pieces (an article, a tips list, a quiz, a how-to), design the pages, and hand out real copies.
need: A topic your kid could talk about for hours
Paper folded into a booklet, pencils, markers, and a stapler (or a computer for layout)
A real magazine to flip through, if you have one

lesson.text: A magazine isn't one long essay. It's short pieces that each do a different job, and each needs a headline that makes someone want to read it.
lesson.before: Article: Dogs. Dogs are animals. They are nice.

model.line: Why Your Dog Tilts Its Head (Scientists Have a Theory)
5 Tricks You Can Teach Any Dog in a Week
What Kind of Dog Are You? Take the Quiz!
Make Peanut Butter Dog Biscuits in 4 Steps

lesson.modelNote: Each fixed headline promises the reader something (a reason, a trick, a result, a recipe), where 'Dogs' just named the topic. Your kid will write one for every page.

howTo.intro: Resist turning editor. Give one suggestion per piece, never a rewrite, and let spelling wait until the design stage.

plan.what: The cover remix game, then choose the topic and plan the issue (Step 1). About 30 minutes.
Research and write the pieces, one or two a day (Steps 2 and 3).
Design the pages, edit, print and hand it out (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid doesn't like writing yet
troubleshoot.a: Lean on short pieces: a quiz, a top 5 list, a comic, a labelled diagram. They count.

troubleshoot.q: Your kid is 6 or 7, or it feels too big
troubleshoot.a: Make it one folded sheet: an 8-page zine of drawings with labels, a mini quiz and a top 3 list. That's a real magazine.

troubleshoot.q: It stalls halfway through the week
troubleshoot.a: Shrink the issue, not the deadline. Publish the finished pieces with a cover as Issue 1, and save the rest for Issue 2.

steps.title: Remix a magazine cover
steps.why: Rewrite three magazine headlines about the cat, then plan an issue of your own.
steps.kid: Flip through a real magazine (or look one up together) and notice the cover: the big title, the headlines, the picture. Your kid rewrites 3 of the headlines about something silly, like the family cat or Tuesday's dinner. Then they pick their own magazine topic, decide who it's for, and plan the issue: a list of pieces, each labelled by type, in a rough table of contents.
steps.you: Play the remix game too, and laugh. Then help them think of a topic they could talk about for hours, and check they could write at least 4 different pieces about it. Aim for a mix: something long, something short, something interactive.
ask: What makes you want to pick up a magazine?
Who's the reader: kids your age, younger kids, grown-ups?
steps.tip: Give the magazine a real name before anything is written. It makes the whole project feel official.

levels.explore: Remix one headline out loud, pick a topic, and draw 3 boxes for 3 pieces with a picture in each.
levels.develop: Plan 4 or 5 pieces in at least 3 different types, with a rough table of contents.
levels.extend: Plan the issue for a reader who knows nothing about your topic. Put the pieces in reading order: what does that reader need first?

steps.title: Research the facts
steps.why: Even a fun magazine needs true information.
steps.kid: Your kid works out which pieces need facts (articles, fact pages, how-tos) and finds 2 or 3 for each, from books, websites or a person who knows. They note where each fact came from. If there's an interview piece, they plan the questions and do the interview.
steps.you: Help find sources if needed. Ask the checking questions: is that true? Where did you find it? Can you check it in a second place?
ask: Is there a surprising fact that would make a great opening?
Can you check that fact somewhere else?
steps.tip: One surprising fact makes a whole article. 'Octopuses have three hearts' does more work than ten ordinary ones.

levels.explore: Find 1 or 2 facts for your main article. A grown-up can read the book aloud, or ask someone who knows.
levels.develop: Find facts for each piece that needs them, and check the key ones.
levels.extend: For each fact, find a second source that agrees. If two sources disagree, say which you trust and why.

steps.title: Write the pieces
steps.why: Your kid writes each piece in its own style, with a headline that makes you read it.
steps.kid: Your kid writes each piece in full, matching the style to the job: factual for articles, friendly for tips, fun for quizzes, clear and numbered for how-tos. Each gets a headline like the examples at the start. They add an 'about the editor' box with a short bio.
steps.you: Read each piece on its own and give one specific suggestion: 'This article needs a stronger opening' or 'Your quiz needs one more question.' Then let them fix it.
ask: Does your first sentence make someone want to keep reading?
Would you actually want to take this quiz?
steps.tip: One or two pieces a day keeps it fun. Writing the whole magazine in one sitting is how it turns into a chore.

levels.explore: Make 2 or 3 short pieces with headlines. Telling a grown-up the words counts.
levels.develop: Write 4 or 5 pieces in different styles, each with a clear headline written for your reader.
levels.extend: Each page fits only 100 words. Write each piece long, then cut it to fit without losing the best line.

steps.title: Design the pages and edit
steps.why: The pieces become a magazine someone would pick up, then get polished.
steps.kid: Your kid designs the cover (title, a main headline, a picture), lays out each piece on its page with headings and illustrations, and makes a table of contents. Then they read the whole magazine like a first-time reader and fix anything unclear, messy or unfinished, including spelling.
steps.you: Help with practical layout if needed. Ask the reader's questions: is the text big enough? Does the cover grab you? Then be the final reader, mark anything that confused you, praise what works, and suggest one fix per page.
ask: Would you pick up this magazine from the cover alone?
Is there enough white space, or does every page feel crowded?
steps.tip: Fold the paper into a booklet before laying anything out. It's much easier to see what goes on which page.

levels.explore: Make a cover, put each piece on a page with a heading, and fix anything messy.
levels.develop: Add a table of contents and matching illustrations, then do a full edit with someone else's feedback.
levels.extend: Give it to someone who doesn't know your topic and watch where they slow down or skip. Fix those pages first.

steps.title: Publish it and look back
steps.why: Copies go out to readers, and your kid hears what they think.
steps.kid: Your kid assembles the magazine (staple, fold or bind), makes copies, and hands them out to at least 2 or 3 people. They ask which piece readers liked best. Then they think about which kind of writing was hardest, and what a second issue would include.
steps.you: Help with copies, then celebrate. A whole magazine, researched, written, designed and published, is a big deal. Ask what they're most proud of and which piece was hardest.
ask: Which piece got the best reaction from readers?
If you made a second issue, what would you change?
steps.tip: Hand-delivered copies feel like a real launch. Let your kid do the handing out.

levels.explore: Share the magazine with one person and tell them your favourite piece.
levels.develop: Share it with 2 or 3 people and ask each which piece they'd cut. Decide if you agree, and why.
levels.extend: Note which piece each reader turned to first, and plan Issue 2 around that.

conclusion.headline: Their magazine is out, and people read it.
conclusion.text: Hand them a magazine at the library or the shop and ask which headline they'd read first, and why. Then see if they can tell you what kind of piece each one is: an article, a tips list, a quiz.
conclusion.celebrate: When a reader stops on a page and reads a line out loud, catch your kid's eye and say: 'That headline did its job. They stopped right there.'
extensions: Make Issue 2, with new pieces on the same topic
Team up with a sibling or friend on a joint issue
Make a digital version on a computer
Start a regular magazine with a new issue each season

signs: They notice headlines and covers when you're out
They change how they write depending on who it's for
They plan big projects in pieces instead of all at once
makeItReal: Get the magazine into real readers' hands outside the family: leave copies at the library's community shelf, mail one to a grandparent, or trade issues with a friend who makes one too.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.caption: My son's article on the Panama Canal, published for family and friends.

fromHome.text: During our seven months of travel, my kids published their own pages on our family travel website for every country. My son wrote a researched article on the Panama Canal that opens with a hook: in a normal year, about 14,000 ships cross it. My daughter wrote about the jungle birds and animals of a national park, then a piece on how Panamanians celebrate Christmas. Family and friends back home read every one.
